response.content:
# SSA Construction

## Dominance Frontiers and the CFRWZ Algorithm

The classical algorithm of Cytron, Ferrante, Rosen, Wegman, and Zadeck (CFRWZ, 1991) builds minimal (in a precise technical sense) SSA form in two phases: phi-placement and renaming, both driven by dominance information.

A node `d` dominates node `n` if every control-flow path from the entry to `n` passes through `d`. The dominator tree encodes this as a tree where each node's parent is its immediate dominator (idom), the unique closest strict dominator. It is typically computed with the Lengauer-Tarjan algorithm (near-linear, O(E log V)) or, in modern compilers, the simpler iterative Cooper-Harvey-Kennedy algorithm that computes dominance via repeated intersection of predecessors' dominator sets until fixpoint, which in practice runs in near-linear time on CFGs.

The dominance frontier of a node `n`, DF(n), is the set of nodes `z` such that `n` dominates a predecessor of `z` but `n` does not strictly dominate `z` itself. Intuitively, DF(n) is where n's dominance "runs out" — exactly the join points where a definition reaching along one path must be merged with a definition (or lack thereof) from another path. CFRWZ computes DF(n) for every node using a bottom-up walk of the dominator tree with the recurrence:

DF(n) = DFlocal(n) ∪ ⋃_{c ∈ children(n)} { w ∈ DF(c) : idom(w) ≠ n }

Here DFlocal(n) covers successors of n in the CFG that n does not strictly dominate, and the second term propagates "up" frontier nodes from children that are not themselves dominated by n. This computes all dominance frontiers in O(N²) worst case (quadratic in pathological CFGs) but near-linear in practice.

For phi-placement, for every variable `v` with a set of definition blocks Defs(v), CFRWZ computes the iterated dominance frontier IDF(Defs(v)) — the fixpoint closure of DF under repeated application, since inserting a phi at a frontier node creates a new "definition" that may itself need a phi downstream. A phi for `v` is placed at every block in IDF(Defs(v)). This is the precise condition for placing the minimal set of phis consistent with CFG join structure (minimal SSA, though not necessarily pruned — see below). Renaming then walks the dominator tree, maintaining a per-variable stack of reaching definitions, pushing a new SSA name at each definition/phi and popping on dominator-tree-subtree exit, resolving each use to the top-of-stack name. This correctly uses dominance: a use is always dominated by its unique reaching def in SSA, so dominator-tree-order traversal suffices.

Trade-off: CFRWZ requires full CFG construction, dominator tree, and dominance frontier computation up front — a global, two-pass, non-incremental process. It is the textbook algorithm and underlies many retargetable analyses (dominance frontier info is reusable for other optimizations), but is awkward for incremental or JIT-style construction where the CFG is built on the fly from a syntax-directed walk.

## Braun et al. Simple and Efficient SSA Construction

Braun, Buchwald, Hack, Leißa, Mallon, and Zwinkau (CC 2013) present an alternative that avoids computing dominance frontiers altogether, building SSA directly during a single forward pass over the CFG as it is discovered (e.g., during AST-to-IR lowering), which is attractive for JIT compilers.

The core idea is local value numbering per block combined with recursive, lazy phi insertion. For each block, a map `currentDef[variable, block]` records the current SSA value of a variable in that block. `writeVariable(v, block, value)` just updates this map. `readVariable(v, block)`: if block has a local definition, return it; otherwise recursively resolve from predecessors via `readVariableRecursive`.

The subtlety is handling blocks whose predecessor set isn't fully known yet, because the CFG is being built incrementally (e.g., forward branches, loop headers reached before their back edges exist). Braun et al. introduce the notion of an **incomplete CFG node**: a block is marked unsealed if not all of its predecessors are yet known. For an unsealed block, a placeholder phi (an "operandless" phi) is created to break recursion (critical for loops) and recorded in `incompletePhis[block]`. Once the block is sealed (all predecessors known), `addPhiOperands` is invoked to fill in the phi's operand list by reading the variable from each predecessor.

This produces eager phi insertion at merge points lazily discovered to need them, as opposed to CFRWZ's global precomputation. For a sealed block with exactly one predecessor, `readVariableRecursive` just forwards the value (no phi needed) — this is the trivial-phi elimination built into the algorithm itself: after building a phi, `tryRemoveTrivialPhi` checks whether all its operands are identical (or self-referential), and if so replaces all uses of the phi with the single distinct operand and removes it, recursively propagating this simplification to users. This yields pruned SSA-like minimality without a separate liveness-based pruning pass, though it is not guaranteed minimal in the CFRWZ sense in all cases — it is "sufficiently minimal" in practice and the paper proves it's still correct (no redundant phis beyond what local simplification catches) and that the result coincides with minimal SSA for well-structured programs.

Complexity is roughly linear in program size for well-behaved CFGs, with no separate dominance or dominance-frontier computation required — dominance falls out implicitly from the fact that `readVariable` only ever returns values that are available along all paths. Trade-off versus CFRWZ: no global dataflow prepass, better for single-pass/JIT construction (this algorithm is used in libFirm and influenced many JIT IRs), but the recursive lookup can be less cache-friendly and reasoning about worst-case complexity is less crisp than the dominance-frontier approach; it also doesn't directly give you the dominator tree as a byproduct, which many later passes need anyway.

## Minimal, Pruned, and Semi-Pruned SSA

"Minimal SSA" (CFRWZ's IDF-based placement) places a phi wherever two distinct definitions merge, even if the merged value is never used afterward (dead phi). "Pruned SSA" additionally uses liveness information: a phi for `v` is inserted at block `b` only if `v` is live-in to `b`, eliminating phis for variables whose value isn't subsequently used along any path, which requires a prior (or interleaved) liveness analysis. "Semi-pruned SSA" is a cheap approximation: before phi placement, compute which variables are *ever* live across a block boundary at all (a cheap, often single-pass, global check, not full per-block liveness) and only build SSA for those variables that are "live somewhere non-locally" — local (single-block) temporaries never get phis or renaming machinery at all. This trades a slightly less precise prune for much lower analysis cost, and is the approach used in several production compilers (e.g., early SSA implementations in GCC) as a pragmatic middle ground between unpruned minimal SSA and full liveness-pruned SSA.

## SSA Destruction

Converting SSA back to a conventional (non-SSA) IR for code generation requires eliminating phi nodes, which have no direct hardware correspondent. The naive approach replaces each phi `x = φ(x1 from B1, x2 from B2, ...)` by inserting copies `x := xi` at the end of each predecessor Bi. This is correct only if done carefully because of two classic hazards:

- **The lost-copy problem**: if a variable used in a phi operand is itself redefined later in the same predecessor block after the point where the copy would need semantics "at the branch," naive copy insertion at the very end of the block can pick up the wrong (later-redefined) value. This happens particularly when critical edges exist (edges from a block with multiple successors to a block with multiple predecessors) and the value flowing into the phi is overwritten along that edge's source block before branching.
- **The swap problem**: when two phis in the same block effectively need to exchange values coming from the same predecessor (x gets old y, y gets old x), naively sequential copies clobber one before the other is read, requiring either a temporary or an explicit swap/rotation of registers.

The standard, robust solution (Sreedhar et al., and the approach generalized by Boissinot et al.) is to reason about **phi-congruence classes**: the set of SSA names that a phi node and its operands "want" to share a single storage location/register with, post-destruction. Two SSA values are placed in the same congruence class only if they can be proven non-interfering (their live ranges don't force different values into the same storage at the same time) — this is essentially a graph-coloring-adjacent problem related to but distinct from register allocation's interference graph. Edges are first split (critical edges get an empty basic block inserted) so that copies can always be placed on an edge unambiguously without ordering hazards. Then a copy-insertion phase inserts parallel copies at the end of each predecessor (conceptually simultaneous, resolved via a sequentialization algorithm that detects cycles like the swap problem and breaks them with a temporary register). Finally, a **coalescing** phase merges phi-congruence classes into single variables/registers where safe, eliminating the inserted copies when source and destination can share storage, which is where SSA destruction interacts directly with register allocation — overly aggressive coalescing before allocation can increase register pressure, so modern approaches often interleave or sequence coalescing with the allocator's interference analysis rather than treating destruction as fully separate from register assignment.

---

# Alias Analysis

## Andersen's Inclusion-Based Points-To Analysis

Andersen's analysis (1994) computes, for every pointer-typed variable `p`, a points-to set pts(p) ⊆ Objects, where objects are abstracted allocation sites or named variables. It is formulated as a set of inclusion constraints derived from the program text: for `p = &x`, add `x ∈ pts(p)`; for `p = q`, add `pts(q) ⊆ pts(p)`; for `p = *q`, add a conditional constraint `∀a ∈ pts(q): pts(a) ⊆ pts(p)`; for `*p = q`, add `∀a ∈ pts(p): pts(q) ⊆ pts(a)`. These constraints are naturally represented as a graph (the "points-to graph" or constraint graph) where subset constraints are edges and solving the system is a graph reachability/closure problem: propagate tokens (object labels) along edges until fixpoint, and dereference constraints dynamically add new edges as new points-to facts are discovered (this is why it's "inclusion-based" — it directly tracks subset relationships rather than merging variables).

This is flow-insensitive (one points-to set per variable for the whole program, ignoring program order/control flow) and typically context-insensitive in its basic form. The worst-case complexity is O(n³) where n is the number of variables/constraints, because each of up to O(n²) pairwise subset edges can trigger propagation of up to O(n) points-to facts; in practice cubic-time behavior is rarely hit and the dominant cost is proportional to the total size of points-to sets, which scales much better with set-sharing / BDD-based representations.

Andersen's is strictly more precise than Steensgaard's (below) because it tracks subset/directional flow rather than collapsing aliasing variables into equivalence classes, at the cost of higher complexity.

## Steensgaard's Unification-Based Points-To Analysis

Steensgaard's analysis (1996) achieves near-linear time (effectively O(n) with union-find, O(n α(n)) more precisely) by using **unification** instead of inclusion: whenever an assignment relates two pointers (or a dereference links a pointer to its target), the analysis merges their points-to representations into one equivalence class using a union-find data structure over "type" nodes representing storage locations. Concretely, each variable is mapped to an abstract storage location node with a single outgoing "points-to" edge to another node representing what it may point to; assignments like `p = q` cause the points-to targets of `p` and `q` to be unified (made the same node) rather than merged as a set union. This means if `p` can point to `x` and separately `q` can point to `y`, and later `p = q` occurs, the analysis concludes both `p` and `q` may point to *both* `x` and `y` — a one-way merge in Andersen's would be a subset relation, but Steensgaard permanently and symmetrically fuses the two targets, losing directionality.

The practical trade-off is precision versus speed: Steensgaard's is almost always faster and scales to very large codebases (used historically in tools needing whole-program points-to facts cheaply) but produces substantially coarser (more conservative, more "may-alias") results, since unification can never be undone and errors compound — one spurious unification can cascade into large equivalence classes ("over-unification"). Andersen's, by contrast, allows incremental precision improvements (e.g., adding context- or field-sensitivity) more naturally because its constraint-based formulation composes.

## Type-Based Alias Analysis (TBAA)

TBAA sidesteps points-to set computation entirely and instead uses the *static type* of the memory access as a cheap, unsound-with-respect-to-type-punning but legally justified (under strict aliasing rules in C/C++) proxy for aliasing. The rule, as implemented in LLVM's TBAA metadata, is: two memory accesses may alias only if their declared access types are compatible under the language's aliasing rules (e.g., in C, an `int*` access and a `float*` access to unrelated types cannot alias barring a `char*`/unsigned-char exception). LLVM encodes this as a type-hierarchy metadata tree attached to load/store instructions; the alias query reduces to a tree-ancestry/compatibility check between the two accesses' type nodes, which is O(tree depth) and requires no interprocedural analysis at all — it's a purely syntactic/type-system-driven decision made at the IR level, not a dataflow fixpoint.

This gives TBAA its principal advantage: extremely cheap, highly precise disambiguation for languages with strict aliasing (letting the optimizer treat accesses through different pointer types as non-aliasing, enabling reordering and redundancy elimination that points-to analysis alone wouldn't justify). The well-known trade-off is unsoundness in the presence of undefined-behavior-relying type punning (common in C via unions or `reinterpret_cast`-style casts), which is exactly why strict-aliasing violations are a notorious source of miscompilation bugs — the analysis is correct *given* the language's aliasing rules, but those rules are themselves a contract the programmer can violate.

## Flow-Sensitivity, Context-Sensitivity, and the Alias Lattice

Orthogonal to the choice of Andersen/Steensgaard/TBAA is **flow-sensitivity**: a flow-sensitive analysis computes a separate points-to set (or alias fact) per program point, tracking strong updates (a store `*p = x` can kill prior facts about `*p` when p is known to point to exactly one object) versus flow-insensitive analysis, which computes one global set per variable valid at all points and can only perform weak updates (union, never kill), which is less precise but dramatically cheaper since it avoids per-program-point state (cost scales with CFG size × variable count rather than just variable count).

**Context-sensitivity** addresses precision loss from treating a function's parameters/returns identically across all call sites. Call-string-based context sensitivity distinguishes calling contexts by a bounded-length string of call sites (k-CFA-style, with k often 1 for tractability), while object-sensitivity (common in points-to analysis for object-oriented languages) instead distinguishes contexts by the abstract receiver object a method is invoked on, which scales better for OO code with deep call chains since it ties context to data rather than control flow. Context-insensitive analysis merges all call sites' facts together, which can cause spurious aliasing between unrelated call sites sharing a callee.

**Field-sensitivity** determines whether distinct fields of the same aggregate/struct are tracked separately (field-sensitive, more precise, needed for sound analysis of struct-heavy code) or collapsed into one points-to set for the whole object (field-insensitive, cheaper, used by coarse analyses like basic Steensgaard variants).

The results of any of these analyses are reported along a standard **alias lattice**: `NoAlias` (provably disjoint memory), `MustAlias` (provably always identical location, enabling strong updates and value propagation through pointers), and `MayAlias` (neither provable; must be treated conservatively). This lattice underlies modref (modification/reference) analysis and memory dependence analysis in optimizers like LLVM: a load/store pair is reordered only if modref analysis can show NoAlias (or MustAlias when that permits the optimization, e.g. redundant load elimination), and conservatively serialized under MayAlias.

---

# Escape Analysis

## Connection-Graph-Based Escape Analysis (Choi et al.)

Choi, Gupta, Serrano, Sreedhar, and Midkiff (1999, used as the basis for HotSpot's EA) formulate escape analysis as the construction and propagation of a **connection graph**: a graph whose nodes are abstract objects (one per allocation site, or "Phantom" nodes for objects of unknown origin such as parameters) and local/global reference variables, with edges representing "points-to" and "deferred" (assignment-chain) relationships, analogous in spirit to points-to graphs in alias analysis but specialized for escape classification. The analysis is performed intraprocedurally first, then summarized and composed across call sites (a form of interprocedural summary-based analysis): each method produces a connection graph summary describing how its formal parameters, return value, and newly allocated objects relate, and callers instantiate/merge this summary at each call site, avoiding full call-string context sensitivity while still getting useful interprocedural precision.

An object node is marked as escaping if a path exists in the connection graph from that object to a node representing a location visible outside the current method/thread: stored into a static/global field, stored into another escaping object's field, passed to an unanalyzed call, or returned. This is computed via a fixpoint propagation over the connection graph (escape status propagates along edges until no new node is marked), with complexity driven by graph size (nodes ≈ allocation sites + variables, edges ≈ assignments) and typically near-linear per method with the dominant cost in the interprocedural summary composition.

## NoEscape / ArgEscape / GlobalEscape (HotSpot Classification)

HotSpot's JIT (C2 compiler) classifies each allocation into one of three escape states, directly derived from connection-graph reachability:

- **NoEscape**: the object never escapes the compiled method or any of its inlined callees — no path exists to a global, to the heap via an unanalyzed store, or to a caller via return/output parameter. 
- **ArgEscape**: the object escapes via being passed as an argument to a call that the compiler could not fully analyze (i.e., it may escape through that call), but doesn't provably escape globally — a weaker, call-boundary-local form of escape.
- **GlobalEscape**: the object is stored to a static field, a heap object reachable from outside, or returned to a caller in a way that makes its lifetime unbounded/unknown — the conservative default when no better classification can be proven.

This three-level lattice (rather than a flat escapes/doesn't-escape boolean) lets the compiler apply different optimizations at different confidence levels: NoEscape unlocks the most aggressive transformations (stack allocation, scalar replacement), while ArgEscape still permits some optimizations around synchronization since the object's monitor cannot be observed as shared by another thread even if the object's data escapes structurally.

## Scalar Replacement of Aggregates and Stack Allocation

When an allocation is classified NoEscape, two major transformations become legal. **Stack allocation** converts a heap allocation (normally requiring GC-managed memory) into a stack-frame-local allocation (or in HotSpot's case, since explicit stack allocation of Java objects is awkward with its frame layout, this is usually subsumed by scalar replacement rather than literal stack allocation). **Scalar replacement of aggregates (SRA)** goes further: if an object's fields are only ever accessed through statically-known field accesses (no unanalyzable pointer arithmetic or reflection) and the object doesn't escape, the compiler can eliminate the object entirely and replace each field with an independent SSA-renamed scalar virtual register/variable, exactly as if the fields had been separate local variables all along. This composes directly with SSA construction: after SRA, these synthesized scalars are fed into the ordinary SSA-construction pipeline (mem2reg-style promotion) and subsequently optimized (constant propagation, dead code elimination) as regular values, often eliminating the allocation and all its field accesses completely when the object is small and short-lived (a very common pattern for temporary wrapper/boxed objects, iterator state, and tuple-return idioms).

The trade-off versus always relying on a fast-path allocator/generational GC nursery is that escape analysis is a conservative static approximation — it must be sound (never wrongly classify an escaping object as non-escaping), so any ambiguity (reflection, unanalyzed virtual calls, native/FFI boundaries) forces conservative GlobalEscape classification, meaning real-world benefit is limited to allocations with simple, provably-local lifetimes. Precision is also limited by whatever interprocedural depth the summary-and-inlining strategy achieves — HotSpot in practice gets most of its mileage from escape analysis in combination with aggressive inlining, since inlining exposes callee behavior directly into the connection graph rather than relying on a coarser method summary.

## Synchronization Elimination (Lock Elision)

If an object is proven NoEscape (or even just not shared across threads despite ArgEscape, since argument-escape to a call doesn't inherently imply multi-thread visibility of the monitor), any `synchronized` block or intrinsic lock operation on that object's monitor can be eliminated entirely, because no other thread can ever observe or contend for a lock on an object only one thread can reach. HotSpot's C2 implements this directly from the same connection-graph escape classification used for scalar replacement: a lock/unlock pair on a NoEscape object is simply removed from the compiled code, eliminating the associated memory barrier and CAS (compare-and-swap) overhead. This is a clean example of a single static analysis result (escape classification) feeding multiple distinct backend transformations (allocation elimination, synchronization elimination) rather than needing separate analyses for each.

## Go's Compiler Escape Analysis and Partial Escape Analysis (Graal)

Go's compiler performs escape analysis as a mandatory part of normal compilation (not just a JIT speculative optimization) to decide, for every allocation (explicit `new`, composite literal, or closure capture), whether it can be placed on the goroutine's stack or must be heap-allocated with GC tracking. The analysis is essentially the same connection-graph-style reachability idea: if a pointer to the allocated value can be shown to flow only within the current function's stack frame and its callees up to a provable depth (and doesn't get stored into a heap-reachable location, returned by pointer in a way that outlives the frame, or captured by an escaping closure/goroutine), it's stack-allocated; otherwise it escapes to the heap. Because Go lacks a JIT and must make this decision once at ahead-of-time compile time without runtime profile feedback, it tends to be more conservative than HotSpot's EA for ambiguous cases (e.g., passing a pointer to an interface method call often forces heap allocation unless the compiler can devirtualize), which is why idiomatic Go performance advice includes avoiding unnecessary pointer indirection and interface boxing to help the escape analysis succeed.

Graal's **partial escape analysis** generalizes the binary escapes/doesn't-escape classification to control-flow paths: rather than requiring an object to be non-escaping along *every* path from allocation to method exit in order to apply scalar replacement, partial escape analysis performs the transformation speculatively along paths where the object provably doesn't escape and only materializes the actual heap object ("deoptimizes" the virtual object into a real allocation) lazily, at the specific control-flow point where escape first becomes unavoidable (e.g., one branch of an if/else stores the object into a global, the other doesn't). This is implemented via Graal's graph-based IR representing the object's fields as "virtual object" nodes that are merged/materialized on demand at control-flow join points, effectively combining scalar replacement with a sparse conditional analysis rather than requiring a single whole-method escape verdict. This captures significantly more real-world cases (objects that escape only on a rare error path, for instance) than a method-granularity classification like HotSpot's, at the cost of a more complex implementation that must handle materialization correctly at arbitrary merge points, including reconstructing the object's state from whichever virtual fields were live along the taken path.

# Register Allocation

## Chaitin-Briggs Graph-Coloring Register Allocation

Graph-coloring register allocation models the allocation problem as coloring an **interference graph** G = (V, E), where V is the set of live ranges (or virtual registers) and an edge (u,v) ∈ E exists iff u and v are simultaneously live at some program point and cannot occupy the same physical register. If k is the number of available physical registers, a valid assignment is a proper k-coloring of G.

**Construction.** The interference graph is built from liveness analysis (a backward dataflow analysis computing LIVE-IN/LIVE-OUT sets per basic block, typically iterated to a fixed point over the CFG). At each program point, every pair of simultaneously-live variables gets an interference edge; definitions interfere with everything live-out of that point except the value they define (to allow coalescing). This is naively O(n²) per point but is usually computed incrementally from live sets using sparse bitsets or a union-find-based live-range structure, which is the standard implementation approach in practice (e.g., via live-range splitting and SSA).

**The simplify/spill/select worklist algorithm.** Chaitin's original algorithm, refined by Briggs, operates as follows:

1. **Build**: construct the interference graph and compute degree(v) for each node.
2. **Simplify**: repeatedly remove ("push onto a stack") any node with degree < k. Removing a low-degree node cannot cause it to fail coloring later, since fewer than k neighbors leaves at least one free color regardless of their colors.
3. **Spill** (when no node has degree < k): heuristically pick a candidate for spilling based on a cost/degree ratio (see below), mark it as a *potential* spill, and remove it from the graph to let simplification continue. Chaitin's original scheme commits to spilling at this point; Briggs's **optimistic coloring** defers the decision.
4. **Select**: pop nodes off the stack in reverse order, assigning each the lowest available color not used by its already-colored neighbors (which number < k, so a color is guaranteed to exist for nodes removed during simplify).
5. **Actual spill**: for nodes marked potential-spill that fail to get a color during select (because all k colors are taken by already-colored neighbors), insert spill code (loads/stores to memory) and rebuild the interference graph for the modified program, iterating the whole pipeline.

**Optimistic coloring (Briggs)** is the key refinement: rather than assuming a high-degree node will definitely need to spill, it is pushed onto the stack anyway. When popped during select, many of its neighbors may have been colored with overlapping colors or may themselves have been spilled, so a free color might still exist. This reduces unnecessary spilling significantly compared to Chaitin's pessimistic approach, at negligible extra cost (same O(V+E) amortized structure, just a different spill decision point).

**Spill cost heuristics.** The candidate chosen during the spill step is typically the node minimizing cost(v)/degree(v), where cost(v) approximates the runtime overhead of spilling (weighted by estimated execution frequency, e.g., loop nesting depth multiplied by a constant per use/def) and degree(v) estimates how much spilling that node will relieve pressure. This ratio favors spilling low-use, high-interference variables (e.g., long live ranges spanning many other values) over frequently-used ones.

**Complexity**: graph coloring is NP-complete in general, so this is a heuristic; the algorithm itself runs in roughly O(V² ) to O(V·E) per iteration due to degree updates, with possibly multiple build/color iterations until no spills are needed.

## Chaitin-Briggs vs. Chow-Hennessy Priority-Based Allocation

Chow-Hennessy's **priority-based allocation** takes a fundamentally different approach: rather than building a general interference graph and coloring it, it computes a priority for each live range based on its estimated benefit (reduced spill/reload cost weighted by loop depth) divided by its size (live range length, affecting how much it blocks other allocations). Live ranges are processed in priority order; each is assigned a register if one is free across its entire extent, otherwise it may be **split** into smaller live ranges (at points like loop boundaries) to fit available registers, with spill code inserted only for the unallocated pieces.

The key differences: Chaitin-Briggs treats allocation as a global coloring problem solved all-at-once via graph structure, uniformly handling spill and color decisions through the interference graph; Chow-Hennessy is priority-driven and incorporates live-range splitting as a first-class mechanism rather than a post-hoc repair, often producing better code for architectures with irregular register classes (e.g., some registers reserved for specific purposes) since it can reason locally about each candidate's constraints. Chaitin-Briggs tends to be conceptually cleaner and is the basis for most modern SSA-aware allocators, while Chow-Hennessy's explicit splitting foreshadows the live-range splitting techniques integrated into modern allocators (including LLVM's greedy allocator).

## Coalescing Strategies

Coalescing merges the live ranges of two variables connected by a copy instruction (move) into a single node, eliminating the copy if they can share a register. Naive (**aggressive**) coalescing merges any non-interfering pair, but this can increase the degree of the merged node enough to make the graph non-k-colorable, inducing spills that wouldn't otherwise occur.

**Conservative (Briggs) coalescing** merges u and v only if the resulting merged node has fewer than k neighbors of degree ≥ k (i.e., at most k high-degree neighbors), which is sufficient to guarantee the merged node won't prevent a valid coloring, since high-degree neighbors are the only ones that might all need distinct colors.

**George's conservative rule** is an alternative sufficient condition: merge u and v if every neighbor of u either already interferes with v or has degree < k — a different, sometimes tighter test.

**Iterated Register Coalescing (George & Appel)** interleaves coalescing with the simplify/spill worklist rather than doing all coalescing before or after coloring. Nodes are classified into worklists (simplify, freeze, spill, coalesce); the algorithm alternates simplification (removing low-degree nodes), conservative coalescing (merging safe candidates), freezing (giving up on coalescing a move when neither test applies, to unblock simplification), and spilling, repeating until the graph is resolved. This tight interleaving captures more legal coalesces than doing coalescing as a separate pre-pass, since simplification changes degrees and may enable coalesces (or vice versa) that were previously unsafe.

**SSA-based coalescing** exploits the fact that programs in SSA form have interference graphs that are **chordal** (see below), and that φ-functions/parallel copies at SSA merge points generate many move instructions whose coalescing is essential to avoid excessive copy overhead; because chordal graphs are colorable in linear time and have well-understood structure, coalescing decisions can be made with simpler, provably-correct tests than in the general non-SSA case.

## Linear Scan Register Allocation (Poletto & Sarkar)

Linear scan trades allocation quality for speed, targeting JIT compilers where compile time matters as much as code quality. It computes **live intervals**: for each virtual register, a single contiguous range [start, end] over a linearized instruction numbering (not necessarily a precise liveness set, since control flow is flattened into a single linear order, usually via a reasonable CFG linearization). This approximation sacrifices precision — a value live only in parts of a loop may be treated as live across the whole thing — but makes allocation an interval-scheduling problem.

The algorithm sorts intervals by start point and scans left to right maintaining an **active set** of intervals currently holding a register, ordered by end point. At each new interval's start, it expires (removes) active intervals that have ended, and if a free register remains, assigns it; otherwise it spills the active interval with the furthest end point (a greedy heuristic minimizing the register-occupied span lost). This runs in O(n log n) with sorted interval lists and a priority queue, versus the effectively worse-than-linear practical cost of graph coloring (interference graph construction alone is at least O(V·liveness)).

Linear scan sacrifices optimality — it can spill when graph coloring would have found a valid assignment via smarter interaction accounting — but its speed and simplicity make it standard in JIT environments like the JVM's HotSpot client compiler and early JavaScript engines, where compile latency directly affects program startup.

## SSA-Based / Chordal Graph Coloring (Hack & Goos)

Hack, Grund, and Goos observed that the interference graph of a program in strict SSA form (where every variable has exactly one definition and live ranges respect SSA dominance properties) is **chordal**: every cycle of length ≥ 4 has a chord (an edge connecting two non-adjacent cycle vertices). Chordal graphs are **perfect graphs**, meaning their chromatic number equals their clique number, and critically, they can be colored optimally in linear time O(V+E) via a **perfect elimination ordering** (computable by maximum cardinality search), rather than relying on heuristic simplify/spill.

This matters because it replaces the heuristic, NP-complete-in-general coloring problem with an exact polynomial algorithm, as long as SSA form is preserved during allocation. The catch is that physical register constraints (e.g., calling conventions, fixed register assignments for specific instructions) and spilling must be handled while maintaining chordality, and coalescing moves (which merge SSA values) can destroy the chordal property if done carelessly — hence the careful SSA-aware coalescing criteria discussed above. This approach underlies several modern allocators that perform allocation directly on SSA form before converting out of SSA (SSA destruction), interleaving spilling, splitting, and coloring as a unified pipeline rather than Chaitin-Briggs's iterate-until-fixed-point loop.

## Spilling, Live-Range Splitting, and Rematerialization

**Spilling** inserts store/load pairs around a live range, allocating stack slots for values that cannot get a register. The cost of a spill is roughly proportional to the number of dynamic uses/defs along the spilled range, weighted by estimated execution frequency (loop depth heuristics, or precise profile data when available).

**Live-range splitting** breaks one long live range into multiple shorter ones connected by moves (often at loop boundaries or basic block boundaries), so that only the "hot" portion needs a register while cooler portions can reside in memory or be assigned a different register, reducing register pressure locally without a full spill. This is the core idea generalized from Chow-Hennessy and used extensively in modern allocators like LLVM's greedy allocator, which performs iterative splitting at increasingly fine granularity (basic block, then individual instructions) before resorting to spill.

**Rematerialization** avoids spilling a value by instead recomputing it from other already-available values (e.g., reloading a constant or recomputing an address expression) when cheaper than a spill/reload pair. This requires the compiler to track which values have "cheap" recomputation (pure, side-effect-free expressions with live operands) and to compare recomputation cost against memory traffic cost — often a clear win for simple constants or address computations, since it avoids both the store and the memory round-trip of a load.

**Register pressure** — the number of simultaneously live values at a program point relative to k — governs where spills/splits are necessary; compilers often compute pressure directly from liveness sets and use it to guide instruction scheduling (reordering to reduce overlapping live ranges) as well as allocation, illustrating the coupling between these two optimization phases.

---

# Instruction Scheduling

## List Scheduling with a Data Dependence Graph

List scheduling is the dominant technique for reordering instructions within a scheduling region to exploit instruction-level parallelism (ILP) while respecting true dependences, typically applied after instruction selection and before (or interleaved with) register allocation.

**Data Dependence Graph (DDG) construction.** Nodes are instructions; edges represent:
- **True (flow) dependences** (RAW — read-after-write): instruction B reads a value instruction A writes.
- **Anti-dependences** (WAR — write-after-read) and **output dependences** (WAW — write-after-write): false dependences induced by register/memory reuse, which can sometimes be eliminated by renaming.
- Edges are labeled with a **latency** — the minimum number of cycles that must elapse between the issue of the source and destination instructions (reflecting pipeline/functional-unit latency, e.g., a multi-cycle multiply or a load with cache latency).

Memory dependences require alias analysis to determine whether two memory operations may conflict; when analysis is imprecise, conservative dependence edges are added, limiting reordering opportunities.

**Priority functions.** List scheduling maintains a ready list of instructions whose predecessors in the DDG have already been scheduled, and at each cycle picks the highest-priority ready instruction (subject to resource/functional-unit availability). Common priority heuristics:
- **Critical path length**: the longest latency-weighted path from a node to a DDG sink (leaf); prioritizing nodes with longer remaining critical path minimizes the chance that the critical path becomes the scheduling bottleneck.
- **Latency-weighted priority**: similar, but may weight by node's own latency or by number of dependent successors to favor instructions that unblock the most future work.
- Tie-breaking heuristics include favoring instructions that free registers soonest (to reduce register pressure) or that belong to the original program order (for stability/predictability).

**Algorithm**: cycle-by-cycle simulation, maintaining the ready list as a priority queue; at each cycle, select as many ready, resource-compatible instructions as the machine's issue width allows, then update the ready list by adding newly-ready successors (indegree-zero removal in a topological sort sense). This is O(n log n) for a basic block with n instructions, dominated by maintaining the priority queue, with DDG construction costing O(n²) in the worst case for unconstrained alias analysis (or better with sparse dependence tracking).

**Local vs. global scheduling.** Basic-block (local) list scheduling is restricted to a single basic block, bounded by its entry and exit, which limits available ILP in code with small basic blocks (common in control-heavy code). **Global scheduling** extends the scope across basic block boundaries — moving instructions above or below branches — to find more parallelism, at the cost of needing to handle control dependences and potentially duplicate code (compensation code) when an instruction is speculated past a branch it wasn't originally on both sides of.

## Trace Scheduling (Fisher)

Trace scheduling, developed for early VLIW machines, generalizes list scheduling to a **trace** — a single predicted frequently-executed path through multiple basic blocks, selected using profile data or heuristics (e.g., always-taken loop back edges). The scheduler treats the trace as if it were one large basic block, applying list scheduling across all its instructions and exploiting ILP across what were originally separate blocks.

The complication is **off-trace control flow**: side entrances (jumps into the middle of the trace from outside) and side exits (branches out of the trace to other code) require **compensation code** to preserve correctness when an instruction has been moved across a trace boundary. If an instruction is hoisted above a branch that exits the trace, and that instruction's effect wouldn't have occurred on the off-trace path in the original program, compensation code must be inserted on the off-trace edge to redo or undo that effect, ensuring semantic equivalence to the original program regardless of which path is actually taken at runtime.

This speculative execution (moving instructions past branches, including past points where their legality depends on which branch is taken) requires either hardware support for safely discarding results of speculated instructions that shouldn't have executed (e.g., poison bits, non-trapping speculative loads) or careful compensation code insertion; it works best when traces are selected accurately (so compensation code is rarely executed) and trades increased code size (potentially exponential blowup if traces overlap extensively, since each trace gets its own scheduled copy of the code) for higher achieved ILP versus naive basic-block scheduling.

## Superblock and Hyperblock Scheduling with If-Conversion

**Superblock scheduling** simplifies trace scheduling by first performing **tail duplication**: any side entrance into the middle of a trace is eliminated by duplicating the code from that entry point onward, producing a single-entry, multiple-exit region (a superblock). This removes the need for compensation code on side-entry merges (since there are none), leaving only side-exit compensation code to handle, substantially simplifying the bookkeeping versus full trace scheduling while retaining most of its benefit.

**Hyperblock scheduling** goes further by applying **if-conversion**: conditional branches within a region are converted into predicated instructions (guarded by a boolean predicate register, executing only if the predicate is true, else behaving as a no-op), merging multiple control-flow paths (then and else branches) into a single predicated block with no internal branches. This exposes much greater scheduling freedom since predicated instructions from both sides of a former branch can now be freely reordered and scheduled together (as long as resource constraints and true dependences are respected), at the cost of executing some instructions that produce discarded results (wasted issue slots / wasted execution) — a worthwhile trade-off when branch misprediction cost and control dependence overhead outweigh the wasted work, particularly on VLIW/EPIC architectures (e.g., Itanium) with explicit predicate registers.

## Software Pipelining and Modulo Scheduling (Rau)

**Software pipelining** restructures a loop so that instructions from different loop iterations are overlapped, analogous to hardware pipelining but done statically by the compiler: a steady-state kernel executes slices of several logically-overlapping iterations simultaneously, bracketed by a **prologue** (ramp-up, filling the pipeline) and **epilogue** (drain, finishing partially-completed iterations).

**Modulo scheduling** is the dominant formulation (Rau and Glaeser). The loop body is scheduled once for a repeating pattern with period equal to the **Initiation Interval (II)** — the number of cycles between the start of successive iterations. The compiler seeks the **Minimum Initiation Interval (MII)**, a lower bound derived from two constraints:

- **Resource-constrained MII (ResMII)**: for each functional unit type, the total resource usage per iteration divided by the number of available units of that type, maximized over unit types — i.e., the bottleneck resource's throughput requirement.
- **Recurrence-constrained MII (RecMII)**: for each cycle in the DDG (arising from loop-carried dependences, e.g., an accumulator updated each iteration), the sum of latencies around the cycle divided by the number of iterations spanned by that cycle (the distance), maximized over all cycles — a lower bound imposed by the sequential nature of loop-carried recurrences that cannot be pipelined away.

MII = max(ResMII, RecMII). The scheduler attempts to construct a valid schedule with II = MII using **modulo resource reservation tables** (checking, for each candidate cycle slot modulo II, whether the needed resource is free across all overlapping iterations); if scheduling fails, II is incremented and scheduling is retried, since a larger II relaxes both resource and recurrence pressure. This commonly uses heuristic list-scheduling techniques adapted to the modulo constraint (e.g., **iterative modulo scheduling**, inserting and possibly backtracking/ejecting previously scheduled instructions when conflicts arise).

A key side effect is increased **register pressure**: because multiple iterations' worth of live values are simultaneously active in the overlapped kernel, software-pipelined loops often require more registers than the original loop, sometimes necessitating rotating register files (hardware support found in machines like the Itanium) or explicit code to manage the increased pressure, illustrating again the entanglement between scheduling and allocation.

## Sethi-Ullman Algorithm (Historical)

The Sethi-Ullman algorithm, originally designed for optimal code generation from expression trees on register machines, computes the minimum number of registers needed to evaluate an expression tree without spilling, and produces an evaluation order (labeling) accordingly. Each node is labeled bottom-up with the number of registers required to evaluate the subtree rooted there assuming optimal ordering; at each node, the child requiring more registers is evaluated first (since evaluating the cheaper subtree first would force holding its result in a register while the more demanding subtree is evaluated, wasting register capacity). This labeling, done in a single bottom-up pass (O(n) in tree size), both determines register need and gives a provably optimal evaluation order for tree-shaped expressions with no common subexpressions.

It's primarily of historical and pedagogical interest: it predates and is a precursor to modern instruction scheduling and register allocation as separate, more general phases, and its scope is limited to expression trees (not general DAGs or control flow), but its core insight — evaluate the more register-hungry subexpression first to minimize simultaneous live values — foreshadows the register-pressure-sensitive heuristics used in modern priority-based list scheduling.

## Interaction Between Scheduling and Register Allocation (Phase Ordering)

Instruction scheduling and register allocation have conflicting goals that make their relative ordering a genuine **phase-ordering problem**:

- Scheduling for maximum ILP tends to lengthen live ranges (spreading a definition and its uses further apart to fill schedule slots), increasing register pressure and provoking more spills.
- Register allocation, especially when it inserts spill code or forces specific registers (e.g., due to calling conventions or physical register constraints), introduces new dependences and serializations that can invalidate or degrade a previously computed schedule.

Scheduling before allocation (pre-pass scheduling) risks producing schedules that are infeasible under real register constraints, forcing allocation to spill heavily and requiring the scheduler's work to be partially redone around the inserted spill code. Allocation before scheduling (post-pass scheduling) guarantees register feasibility but may serialize independent operations unnecessarily by reusing registers across unrelated live ranges (introducing artificial WAR/WAW anti-dependences that constrain the scheduler).

Common mitigations include: performing scheduling in two passes (an initial pressure-aware pre-pass that heuristically limits how far live ranges are stretched, followed by allocation, followed by a post-pass schedule cleanup); using a unified heuristic that tracks register pressure during list scheduling itself (deprioritizing instructions that would increase pressure beyond the available register count); or integrating the two problems more tightly as in some SSA-based or PBQP-based (partitioned Boolean quadratic programming) frameworks that model allocation and scheduling costs jointly. No fully general optimal solution exists because the combined problem is NP-hard; practical compilers resort to heuristics and empirically-tuned pass ordering specific to the target architecture's register file size and pipeline characteristics.

response.content:
# Loop Vectorization, Inlining, and Loop Optimizations: Technical Deep-Dive

## 1. Loop Vectorization

### SLP vectorization vs. loop-based (outer-loop) vectorization

These are two distinct algorithms that both emit SIMD code but operate on different program structures. **Loop vectorization** (as in LLVM's `LoopVectorize`) takes a single scalar loop body executing N times and transforms it into a loop executing N/VF times, where each iteration of the new loop processes VF (vectorization factor) original iterations in parallel using SIMD instructions. It works on the loop's induction structure directly: it widens the induction variable, replaces scalar memory accesses with vector loads/stores, and widens arithmetic operations lane-wise.

**SLP vectorization** (superword-level parallelism, Larsen & Amarasinghe 2000) instead looks at *straight-line code* — adjacent independent scalar statements within a basic block (or across isomorphic statements in unrolled loop bodies) — and packs them into vector instructions. The algorithm starts from "seed" groups of isomorphic, independent scalar instructions (typically adjacent stores or isomorphic operations reachable from them), then works backward through the def-use chains building "packs" of instructions that can be fused into a vector op, recursively following operands. It builds an SLP tree bottom-up (or top-down from stores) and inserts shuffles/permutes to reconcile non-contiguous packing. SLP generalizes beyond loops to any code with repeated, independent scalar computation (e.g., manually unrolled code, struct-of-arrays math), but it does not restructure loop trip counts; it only vectorizes within existing control flow.

In production compilers both run as separate passes (LLVM runs loop vectorization first, then SLP on the result) because they catch complementary patterns: loop vectorization handles the induction/trip-count dimension, SLP handles instruction-level parallelism within an iteration or unrolled block.

### Dependence analysis for vectorization

Vectorizing a loop by executing multiple iterations concurrently is only legal if no cross-iteration (loop-carried) dependence is violated by reordering. Dependence analysis computes, for pairs of array references inside a loop nest, a **distance vector** (the difference in iteration indices between a dependent read and write, per loop level) and/or a **direction vector** (the sign of that distance per level: `<`, `=`, `>`, or `*` for unknown). A dependence is loop-carried at level k if the distance vector's first nonzero component is at index k.

Two classic decision procedures compute whether a dependence exists for affine subscripts:

- **GCD test**: for a dependence equation of the form `a0 + a1*i1 + ... + an*in = b0 + b1*j1 + ... + bn*jn`, rewrite as a linear Diophantine equation; it has an integer solution iff `gcd(a1,...,an,b1,...,bn)` divides `(b0 - a0)`. This is a necessary (not sufficient) condition — it can prove independence but cannot alone prove dependence, since it ignores loop bounds.
- **Banerjee's test**: bounds the range of the subscript difference `f(i) - f(j)` over the iteration space's rectangular bounds using interval arithmetic (computing minimum and maximum possible values given index bounds), and checks whether zero (or the required dependence distance) falls within that range. It's also a conservative sufficiency test — if zero is outside the computed range, no dependence exists; if inside, a dependence is *possible* but not certain.

Both run in the "may-dependence" style and are used in combination, falling back to more precise but expensive tests (Omega test, exact integer linear programming) only when needed, since full exactness is NP-hard in general and most production compilers accept conservative approximations for speed.

### Vectorization legality and strip-mining

The legality check for a candidate vectorization factor VF ensures that no loop-carried dependence has a distance smaller than VF in the direction that would cause the vectorized (SIMD-parallel) execution to read a value before it's written or vice versa in a way that changes semantics. Concretely, if there's a flow dependence with distance d > 0 (write at iteration i, read at i+d), vectorizing with VF ≤ d is safe since all d iterations-apart elements stay correctly ordered within one vector operation boundary; VF > d would require cross-lane communication the SIMD model doesn't give for free, making the transform illegal without using the distance to cap VF. Loops with no dependence, or only non-loop-carried dependences, are fully vectorizable at any VF supported by the target.

Once a loop is legal to vectorize, the compiler performs **strip-mining** (also called loop sectioning): the single loop of trip count N is split into an outer loop of trip count ⌈N/VF⌉ and an inner "vector body" of fixed trip count VF, where the inner body is then mapped directly onto SIMD instructions. Because N is frequently not an exact multiple of VF, compilers emit a vectorized main loop plus a scalar (or smaller-VF) remainder loop to handle the tail; some targets instead use masked/predicated tail handling to avoid a separate remainder loop entirely.

### Control flow: if-conversion and predication

Loops containing conditional branches (if/else inside the loop body) cannot be vectorized directly because SIMD execution has no native control-flow divergence across lanes. **If-conversion** transforms control-dependent code into straight-line code guarded by boolean masks: a branch `if (c) S` becomes `S` executed unconditionally with its effects "predicated" by the mask value of `c`, typically implemented as a select (`cmov`-like) operation choosing between the computed and original value, or, on targets with native predication (AVX-512 mask registers, ARM SVE, GPU SIMT lanes), as masked loads/stores and masked arithmetic that only commit lanes where the mask bit is set. This converts a control-dependence problem into a data-dependence problem solvable by ordinary vectorization, at the cost of executing both sides of the branch for all lanes (wasted work when the branch is strongly biased) unless the hardware's predicated execution model avoids it.

### Reduction vectorization

Reductions (sum, product, min/max, logical and/or accumulations) create an apparent loop-carried dependence through the accumulator variable on every iteration. Because operations like `+` and `*` are associative and commutative (floating point `+` is not strictly associative, which is why `-ffast-math`/fast-math flags are typically required to vectorize FP reductions without numerical-reproducibility guarantees), the compiler can legally reorder the accumulation: it maintains VF partial accumulators (one per SIMD lane) throughout the vectorized loop body, then performs a **horizontal reduction** at the end — a sequence of shuffle-and-combine operations (e.g., log2(VF) rounds of `shufflevector` + `add`) that collapses the VF partial sums into the scalar result. This pattern is detected by recognizing a PHI node in the loop header whose incoming value is combined with a loop-invariant-free binary op, forming a recognized reduction idiom.

### Gather/scatter and cost-model-driven vectorization selection

When array accesses inside a loop are not unit-stride (e.g., indexed by another array, `a[idx[i]]`), SIMD lanes may each need to load from or store to unrelated addresses. Hardware gather/scatter instructions (AVX2 `vgather`, AVX-512 `vgather`/`vscatter`) load/store VF elements from VF independent addresses in one instruction, at a throughput cost much higher than contiguous vector loads.

LLVM's loop vectorizer uses a **cost model** that, for each candidate VF (powers of two up to the target's maximum vector width, plus sometimes the "interleave factor" for unrolling the vector loop body itself), estimates the total cost of the vectorized loop body: cost of memory operations (contiguous load/store, strided, gather/scatter — each priced differently per target), cost of each arithmetic/vector instruction, and cost of required shuffles/masks/reductions, against the scalar baseline divided by VF. It picks the VF (and unroll/interleave factor) minimizing estimated cycles per element, sometimes rejecting vectorization entirely if predicted cost exceeds the scalar loop's cost (e.g., gather-heavy loops on targets where gather is expensive). This is why vectorization is profitability-gated, not just legality-gated.

---

## 2. Inlining

### Inline cost/benefit heuristics

Inlining replaces a call site with a copy of the callee's body. It eliminates call/return overhead (stack frame setup, argument marshaling, branch misprediction on return) and crucially *exposes the callee's code to further optimization in the specific context of the caller* — but it increases code size, which can hurt instruction-cache behavior and compile time.

LLVM's `InlineCost` analysis computes a numeric cost for each call site by walking the callee's IR and summing a heuristic cost per instruction (simple arithmetic costs little; calls, especially to functions that themselves can't be inlined, cost more; loops add cost to discourage inlining large iterative bodies), then subtracts a "bonus" for simplifications the inliner predicts will become possible post-inlining — for example, if an argument is a compile-time constant at this call site, instructions in the callee that branch on or compute from that constant are given reduced or zero cost under the assumption constant propagation and branch folding will eliminate them. The final cost is compared against a threshold (a inlining budget), modulated by attributes like `inlinehint`, `noinline`, function size, and whether the call site is "cold" per profile data. GCC's inliner (`ipa-inline`) uses an analogous model: it estimates code-size growth (`size_time_table` summarizing per-callee size/time) against a `badness` function balancing growth versus estimated speedup, informed by a growth budget (`--param inline-unit-growth` etc.) capping total program size expansion.

### Call-graph based inlining order: bottom-up vs top-down

Interprocedural inlining decisions are order-sensitive because inlining a callee into a caller can change the caller's size/shape, which affects whether *that* caller should subsequently be inlined elsewhere. **Bottom-up inlining** processes the call graph in reverse topological order (leaves first): each function is fully optimized/inlined-into before being considered as a candidate to inline into its own callers, so inlining decisions at each call site see the function's "final" post-inlining size and behavior. This is the dominant strategy (used by LLVM's default pipeline via the SCC-based `InlinerPass` on Tarjan SCCs of the call graph) because it means a small leaf function's cost is accurately known before deciding whether to replicate it into N callers.

**Top-down inlining** instead starts from entry points/roots and inlines callees into callers before the callees themselves have been fully processed, which can better propagate caller-side context (constant arguments, known call-site hotness) into decisions about further inlining within the newly-inlined code, at the cost of potentially inlining a callee whose own size will later balloon from further inlining into it. Real pipelines sometimes combine both: an initial bottom-up pass for size-stable leaf inlining followed by iterative top-down passes to propagate specialization opportunities.

Call graphs with cycles (mutual/indirect recursion) are handled via SCC (strongly connected component) decomposition: each SCC is treated as a unit, and functions within a cycle are inlined into each other only up to a bounded depth to guarantee termination.

### Recursive inlining control and depth/budget limits

Naively inlining a recursive call site would not terminate (the callee contains a call to itself, which after inlining contains another call to itself, ad infinitum). Compilers bound this with an explicit **inlining depth limit**: a per-call-site or per-function counter tracking how many times a given function has already been inlined along the current inlining chain, refusing further inlining once a threshold (e.g., LLVM's recursive-inlining heuristics cap self-recursive inlining to roughly one or two levels unless profile data strongly justifies more) is reached. Additionally, a global **inlining budget** tracks cumulative code growth for the whole translation unit/module and throttles further inlining once a growth ceiling is approached, preventing compile-time and binary-size blowup even for non-recursive but deeply nested call chains (a inlines b inlines c inlines d...).

### Devirtualization-enabled inlining

Virtual/indirect calls (C++ virtual methods, function pointers) are normally opaque to the inliner because the callee isn't statically known. **Devirtualization** resolves such calls to a concrete target when analysis proves (or strongly predicts) a single possible callee — e.g., via class hierarchy analysis showing a class has no overriding subclasses, or via points-to/type analysis narrowing a function pointer's possible values to one. When analysis can prove a single target exists (full devirtualization), the indirect call is replaced outright with a direct call, which then becomes an ordinary inlining candidate.

When proof isn't possible but a *likely* target is known (e.g., from profile data showing 95% of calls through this call site go to one implementation), compilers emit **speculative (guarded) inlining**: a runtime type/vtable check comparing the actual receiver's type (or function pointer) against the predicted one, with the inlined fast path taken on match and a fallback indirect call on mismatch. This is the static-compiler analog of **inline caches** used in JIT compilers (V8, HotSpot): at a call site, the JIT records the actually-observed receiver type(s) on first execution (monomorphic inline cache), and on subsequent executions checks the cached type/guard and, if matched, jumps directly to a cached, specialized, often-inlined version of the method body — upgrading to polymorphic or megamorphic inline caches (a small list, or a hash-based dispatch) as more types are observed, and falling back to full dynamic dispatch above an observed-type-count threshold.

### Profile-guided inlining using call-site hotness

Static heuristics approximate importance via syntactic size/structure, but real execution frequency is often a better signal. **Profile-guided inlining** (PGO-informed) uses instrumentation- or sampling-collected edge/call-site counts to bias the cost model: hot call sites (high execution frequency relative to the function or program) get a more generous inlining threshold since the call/return overhead savings and specialization benefits recur many times, while cold call sites (including those under `__builtin_expect`-style unlikely paths, or in code regions a sampling profiler shows are rarely executed) are heavily deprioritized or even outlined, since inlining there mostly costs code size for negligible runtime benefit. This directly targets the inliner's cost/benefit trade-off at the granularity that matters — actual dynamic execution count — rather than static structural proxies alone, and is one of the highest-leverage uses of profile data in modern optimizing compilers (both LLVM's PGO-driven `InlineCost` adjustments and GCC's profile-feedback-driven `ipa-inline`).

### Inlining's relationship to subsequent optimization

Inlining is frequently described as an "enabling transformation" rather than an optimization that saves time on its own merits: its main value is that it moves the callee's code into a context where interprocedural facts (specific argument values, aliasing relationships, call-site-specific control flow) become local facts the rest of the pipeline can exploit. After inlining a call with a constant argument, **constant propagation** can replace parameter uses with the literal, which then enables **constant folding** of downstream arithmetic, which enables **branch folding** of conditions now known statically, which enables **dead code elimination** of now-unreachable branches, and so on, often cascading into significant size reduction that can partially or fully offset the code growth inlining itself introduced. This is why inlining is typically scheduled early and iteratively interleaved with cleanup passes (SCCP, instcombine/GVN, DCE) in modern pipeline structures (e.g., LLVM's pass manager runs an inlining-then-cleanup loop across the module) rather than as a single one-shot pass.

---

## 3. Loop Optimizations

### Loop-invariant code motion (LICM)

LICM identifies computations inside a loop whose operands are all defined outside the loop (or are themselves loop-invariant), and hoists them to the loop preheader so they execute once instead of once per iteration. The analysis requires the loop be in a form with a single-entry **preheader** block; an instruction is invariant if all of its operands are either constants, defined outside the loop, or are other instructions already proven invariant — computed via a straightforward fixpoint/worklist traversal over the loop body in reverse postorder, iterating until no further instructions can be marked invariant. Hoisting is only legal if the instruction has no side effects that depend on iteration count (no stores that could alias with other loop memory operations, unless alias analysis proves safety) and, for loads, if the memory location is provably not modified anywhere in the loop (often via `MemorySSA` or alias analysis queries). LICM also handles **sinking**: moving invariant-but-only-used-after-loop-exit computations to loop exit blocks, and store-sinking of invariant stores to loop exits when safe. Its benefit scales with loop trip count; the risk is register pressure increase in the preheader if too much is hoisted (mitigated by only hoisting profitable, i.e., non-trivial, computations).

### Loop unrolling: full vs. partial

Unrolling replicates the loop body k times (the **unroll factor**) and adjusts the induction variable increment accordingly, reducing the number of branch/loop-control instructions executed relative to work done and enlarging the scheduling window available to the instruction scheduler. **Full unrolling** replicates the entire loop body for every iteration when the trip count is a known compile-time constant, eliminating the loop entirely (no branch, no induction variable) — practical only for small, fixed trip counts since code size grows linearly with trip count. **Partial unrolling** replicates the body k times within a loop that still iterates ⌈N/k⌉ times, requiring a remainder/epilogue loop (or peeling) when N isn't an exact multiple of k, analogous to vectorization's strip-mining remainder handling.

Unrolling interacts strongly with instruction scheduling and vectorization: a larger unrolled body gives the scheduler (list scheduling, software pipelining) more independent instructions to interleave and hide latency, and SLP vectorization specifically depends on unrolling (or its own iteration-merging) to create the isomorphic adjacent-statement groups it packs into vectors. Vectorizers themselves often perform an internal "interleaving" (effectively partial unrolling of the vector loop) to improve memory-level parallelism, choosing an interleave factor as part of the same cost-model search used for VF selection.

### Loop fusion and fission/distribution

**Loop fusion** merges two adjacent loops with compatible iteration spaces (matching trip counts/bounds, provably no new dependence violations introduced by interleaving their bodies) into a single loop, improving locality (data touched by both loops' bodies is now reused while still resident in cache, if it was previously evicted between separate loop passes) and amortizing loop overhead. Legality requires checking that no dependence runs from the second loop's body backward into the first loop's later iterations in a way the fused ordering would violate — formally, fusion-preventing dependences are those where fusing would reverse the relative execution order of a dependent pair.

**Loop fission (distribution)** is the inverse: splitting one loop with multiple independent statement groups into separate loops, each with a subset of the original statements, used when a single combined loop body is not vectorizable (e.g., due to a dependence cycle involving only some of its statements) but a split version isolates the problematic statements into their own loop while leaving the rest vectorizable, or to enable other transformations requiring the isolated loop shape.

### Loop interchange for locality

For a nested loop (typically a doubly- or multiply-nested loop over array indices), **interchange** swaps the nesting order of two loop levels, e.g., turning `for i: for j: A[i][j]` into `for j: for i: A[i][j]`, to change the stride pattern of memory accesses to match the array's storage order (row-major vs. column-major), converting a loop with large, cache-unfriendly stride into one with unit-stride, sequential accesses that fit cache lines efficiently. Legality is determined via the loop nest's **direction/distance vector** dependence information: interchange is legal only if there's no dependence direction vector that, after the swap, has a `>` (reversed) direction in a position preceding a `<` — concretely, interchange is illegal when it would reverse the relative execution order of a dependent pair of iterations. Profitability is determined by a cache-reuse/stride cost model, sometimes integrated into a more general affine scheduling search (see polyhedral discussion below) rather than considered as an isolated discrete choice.

### Loop tiling/blocking for cache locality

**Tiling** (blocking) restructures a loop nest by strip-mining multiple loop dimensions simultaneously and interchanging the resulting strip-mined (tile) loops to be outermost, so that the innermost loops iterate over a small rectangular "tile" of the iteration space small enough that the data it touches fits in cache (L1/L2) and is reused across multiple inner-loop accesses before the tile boundary moves on. This is the standard technique for matrix multiplication and stencil computations where naive loop order causes repeated cache-line evictions; the tile size is chosen (by heuristic or autotuning) to match the target cache capacity divided by the working-set footprint per tile. Tiling trades a more complex loop nest (extra loop levels, boundary/remainder handling for tile sizes not dividing the trip count evenly) for dramatically improved reuse distance, and composes with interchange and fusion within polyhedral frameworks that search the combined transformation space.

### Induction variable recognition and strength reduction

Many loops contain variables that change by a fixed amount each iteration (**induction variables**, IVs) — the canonical loop counter `i`, but also derived IVs like array-indexing expressions `4*i` or `base + i*stride` computed from `i`. Induction variable recognition identifies these patterns, typically represented via the **chains-of-recurrences (chrec)** formalism, `{start, +, step}` notation describing a value's evolution across loop iterations as a (possibly nested, for multi-level loops) affine or polynomial recurrence. Once recognized, **strength reduction** replaces expensive recomputation (e.g., a multiply `4*i` recomputed from scratch each iteration) with an equivalent incremental update (`addr += 4` each iteration, derived from the previous iteration's value) — turning multiplications into additions, which is cheaper on most architectures. LLVM's `ScalarEvolution` analysis builds and canonicalizes these chrec expressions for all IV-derived values in a function, enabling not just strength reduction but also trip-count computation (solving the chrec for when it reaches a bound, used for loop-bound analysis and vectorization's remainder-loop sizing) and dependence-distance computation (subtracting two chrecs for the same array to get the access-distance expression used in dependence testing above).

### Loop-closed SSA form (LCSSA)

LCSSA is a canonical form requirement, not a transformation that changes program behavior: it mandates that every value defined inside a loop and used outside it has a single phi node inserted at the loop's exit block(s) representing that value, so that all uses outside the loop go through this exit phi rather than directly referencing the in-loop definition. This simplifies many loop-transformation passes (LICM, loop rotation, unrolling, interchange, vectorization) because they can reason about "the loop's live-out values" as a clean, enumerable set at well-defined exit points rather than having to trace arbitrary dominance relationships from inside the loop to arbitrary external uses; it also makes the loop's boundary a clean unit that can be cloned, deleted, or re-nested (e.g., for unrolling or interchange) without re-wiring dispersed external uses. Maintaining LCSSA is handled by a dedicated pass that's re-run (or incrementally maintained) whenever a loop transformation might have broken the invariant.

### Polyhedral loop optimization

The **polyhedral model** represents a loop nest's iteration space as an **iteration domain**: a set of integer points satisfying a system of affine inequalities (a polyhedron) over the loop indices, valid for loops with affine bounds and affine array-subscript expressions. Dependences between statement instances are represented as **dependence polyhedra**: for each pair of (possibly different) statements with a potential dependence, the set of iteration-pair points `(i, j)` where instance `i` of one statement and `j` of another access the same memory location with at least one being a write, subject to `i` and `j` satisfying their respective domains and the data-dependence equation — computed via integer linear programming / Presburger arithmetic (exact, unlike the GCD/Banerjee approximations above, at higher computational cost, generally exponential worst case but practical for typical loop nests).

Optimization is then framed as finding an **affine scheduling transformation** — a function mapping each original iteration-domain point to a new multidimensional execution-time vector — that (a) respects all dependence polyhedra (preserves relative execution order of dependent instances) and (b) optimizes some objective (minimizing dependence distances for locality, enabling parallel dimensions, or exposing tileable bands), typically solved via the Pluto/Feautrier scheduling algorithms as linear/integer programming problems over the schedule coefficients. This single affine-scheduling formalism subsumes interchange, fusion, fission, skewing, and tiling as different instances of the schedule search rather than discrete separate passes — giving it strictly more expressive power than applying each named transformation in isolation, at the cost of being restricted to affine (or near-affine, with extensions) loop bounds and subscripts and significantly higher analysis/compile-time cost. **Polly** (LLVM) and **Graphite** (GCC) are production implementations: they extract polyhedral representations (SCoPs — Static Control Parts, maximal regions meeting the affine-loop/affine-access requirements) from IR, run the scheduling optimization, and re-generate loop IR (via CLooG or ISL's AST generator) from the optimized schedule.

### Loop unswitching

When a loop contains a conditional whose condition is loop-invariant (does not change across iterations, e.g., `for i: if (flag) A[i]=... else B[i]=...` where `flag` is not modified in the loop), **unswitching** hoists the conditional outside the loop, duplicating the loop body into two copies — one for each branch of the condition — each specialized to no longer contain the (now externally-decided) check. This eliminates a per-iteration branch, often enabling further optimizations (vectorization, LICM) within each specialized copy that the original mixed-branch body would have blocked, at the cost of code-size duplication proportional to the number of unswitched conditions (multiple unswitchable conditions compound multiplicatively unless the compiler limits unswitching depth/count via a heuristic threshold).
